questions.question: Which of the following best describes the primary goal of establishing a mapping between components of programming languages from different paradigms?

choices.statement: To prove that one paradigm is objectively superior to all others
To compare and contrast the capabilities of languages and determine how the components of one language can be expressed, fully or partially, in another
To automatically translate any program from one language into another without human intervention
To demonstrate that every language is limited to representing only the entities designed for its own paradigm

questions.hint: Mapping is about comparing and expressing, not ranking or automatic translation.

questions.question: A student maps a Java Human class, with attributes name and age and a method getAge(), into C. Which C construct is the most direct counterpart of the class's data attributes?

choices.statement: A struct whose members correspond to the class's fields
A #define macro placed in a header file
A global extern function declaration
A goto label placed before main()

questions.hint: C's way of grouping named fields together.

questions.question: In C, a struct groups data but does not bundle behavior the way a Java class does. Which technique allows a C struct to approximate an object's methods, so that behavior is stored alongside the data?

choices.statement: Declaring all of the struct's variables as static
Using the extern keyword on each member
Including function pointer members in the struct that refer to functions operating on the struct
Declaring the struct inside a for loop

questions.hint: A struct member that stores the address of a function.

questions.question: A C programmer implements a Kidney "method" as void filter(Kidney *self), where the first parameter explicitly receives a pointer to the struct. What does this convention represent in terms of OOP?

choices.statement: An explicit counterpart of the implicit this reference that Java passes to instance methods
An implementation of method overloading
A way to enforce the private access modifier
A replacement for the constructor

questions.hint: Java passes the object to its methods implicitly; C has to do it explicitly.

questions.question: Which statement best explains why a C mapping of an OOP class with private fields and public methods is usually classified as only "Partial"?

choices.statement: C cannot declare variables of any type
C structs cannot contain more than one member
C does not provide language-level access modifiers, so encapsulation can only be imitated by convention or by hiding the struct's definition behind a header, not enforced by the compiler
C cannot define functions that accept pointers as parameters

questions.hint: Think about what C lacks for hiding data.

questions.question: In Prolog, the entity Human with name "Ana" and age 20 is expressed as the fact human(ana, 20). What does this representation convey about the declarative mapping of compound data?

choices.statement: The data is represented as relations asserted to be true, and a collection of such facts takes the place of an object's attribute values rather than a mutable instance in memory
The fact is an object that stores its own methods and mutable state
The fact is a procedure called in sequence from main
The fact is a pointer to a memory address holding the object

questions.hint: Facts are statements asserted to be true, not objects sitting in memory.

questions.question: A Java Human object can change its age field at runtime via setAge(). Which is the best explanation of why reproducing this behavior in pure Prolog (without assert/retract) is classified as "Partial" or "Not feasible"?

choices.statement: Prolog cannot store numeric values
Prolog has no concept of data types at all

Prolog variables, once bound, cannot be reassigned, so in-place mutation of an object's attribute has no direct counterpart; changing state requires asserting and retracting facts, which are side-effecting operations outside the pure declarative model
Prolog requires every fact to be declared inside a class before use

questions.hint: Prolog variables cannot be reassigned once they are bound.

questions.question: In an OOP model, Student extends Person expresses inheritance. Which of the following is the most faithful way to express this relationship in Prolog?

choices.statement: Writing a rule such as person(X) :- student(X)., so that every student is also derived to be a person
Using the extends keyword before the student predicate
Declaring student as a global variable of type person
Using a function pointer from student to person

questions.hint: Express "every student is also a person" as a logical rule.

questions.question: A class Student is related to a class Course by an association: a student enrolls in many courses, and a course has many students. Which declarative representation best preserves this many-to-many association?

choices.statement: A single fact enrolled(student_course) with no arguments
A binary predicate enrolled(StudentID, CourseID) with one fact for each pairing, which can be queried in either direction
A struct embedded inside a Prolog list of integers
A recursive rule with no base case

questions.hint: A many-to-many link works well as one fact per pairing.

questions.question: Consider an aggregation in which a Human "has a" Kidney. In C, which implementation best captures this relationship while preserving the independent lifetime that aggregation implies, as opposed to composition?

choices.statement: Embedding a full Kidney struct as a member, so the kidney is destroyed with its Human
Declaring the Kidney as a local variable of main()
Storing a pointer to a Kidney struct inside the Human struct, so the kidney can exist independently of the human and be shared or reassigned
Replacing the relationship with a #define macro

questions.hint: Aggregation means the part can outlive the whole, so it should not be embedded inside it.

questions.question:
The C loop below finds the maximum of an array. Which line completes the recursive Haskell version?

Expected output:
9

C version:
int max = a[0];
for (int i = 1; i < n; i++)
    if (a[i] > max) max = a[i];

Haskell version:
myMax :: [Int] -> Int
myMax [x] = x
myMax (x:xs) = __________

main :: IO ()
main = print (myMax [3, 9, 4])

choices.statement: min x (myMax xs)
x + myMax xs
myMax xs
max x (myMax xs)

questions.hint: The recursive case compares the head with the maximum of the rest.

questions.question:
The C loop below counts the digits of a number. Which line completes the recursive Haskell version?

Expected output:
4

C version:
int count = 0;
while (n > 0) { count++; n /= 10; }

Haskell version:
digits :: Int -> Int
digits 0 = 0
digits n = __________

main :: IO ()
main = print (digits 4821)

choices.statement: digits (n `div` 10)
1 + digits (n - 10)
n + digits (n `div` 10)
1 + digits (n `div` 10)

questions.hint: Count one digit, then continue with the number divided by 10.

questions.question:
What is the result of the following Prolog query?

likes(alex, pizza).
likes(alex, pasta).
likes(mia, sushi).

?- likes(alex, X).

choices.statement: X = pizza. (and no other solutions)

X = pizza ;
X = pasta.

X = alex ;
X = mia.
false.

questions.hint: Prolog can return every matching answer, one at a time.

questions.question:
What is the result of the following Prolog query?

parent(ana, ben).
parent(ben, cara).
parent(cara, dan).

grandparent(X, Z) :-
    parent(X, Y),
    parent(Y, Z).

?- grandparent(ana, X).

choices.statement: X = ben.
X = cara.
X = dan.
false.

questions.hint: grandparent(ana, X) asks for a child of ana's child.

questions.question:
Which clause completes the sibling rule so that the query succeeds?

Expected query and result:
?- sibling(alex, ben).
true.

parent(mary, alex).
parent(mary, ben).
parent(john, alex).
parent(john, ben).

sibling(X, Y) :-
    __________

choices.statement: parent(X, Y).
parent(P, X), parent(P, Y), X \= Y.
parent(X, P), parent(Y, P), X = Y.
X = Y.

questions.hint: Siblings share a parent and are not the same person.
